en: The subsequent scripture states: "Wisdom is clear and luminous, observing with profound penetration. To explain the meaning of this name:
all the practices cultivated, consisting of immeasurable merit and wisdom, are entirely equal to reality; by accomplishing these, one performs this dedication. Wisdom is luminous...
"Thoroughly understood" means that through contemplating both principle and phenomena, one attains clear and lucid realization.
Regarding "profound observation": when one's practice accords with principle, it is called "profound"; to abide neither in existence nor non-existence is what constitutes "skillful observation."
From here, the ninth [section] clarifies the dedication of liberation that is unbound and unattached.
The Sūtra says:
"All practices and vows are universally cultivated."
To understand this name means to be neither bound by signs nor attached to various views; with mastery over all that one does, one accomplishes this dedication.
"All practices" refers to the various practices such as giving and so forth.
"All aspirations" refers to the vastness of those vows.
These two support one another, for they necessarily arise together.
"Universally cultivating and practicing" means that, through being free from bondage and attachment, one attains liberation and mastery, thereby cultivating all immeasurable practices and vows.
From here follows the tenth, the immeasurable dedication of the light-like dharma-realm.
The Sūtra says:
"One is able to act as a Dharma teacher, taming and guiding sentient beings."
Regarding the explanation of these names: the various practices one cultivates are free from signs and vast, all being equal to the Dharma-realm; thus one accomplishes this dedication.
One who can act as a Dharma-preacher attains unimpeded understanding (*pratisaṃvid*) because they are skillful in transforming and guiding others.
The "Tamer of Sentient Beings" (Puruṣadamyasārathi) preaches according to their respective faculties to bring them into perfect discipline and to bring about vast benefit and happiness.

As the *Avataṃsaka* states: "Like a stainless silk ribbon bound upon his crown, he abides in the rank of Dharma Master and extensively practices the gift of Dharma; giving rise to great compassion, he establishes sentient beings, constantly performing beneficial deeds upon the path to Bodhi without ever ceasing."
"Nurturing roots of goodness through the bodhicitta and acting as a guide for all sentient beings, showing all sentient beings the path to omniscience"—
this demonstrates the practice of transformative benefit.

It is summarized in verse as follows: "Protecting, indestructible, and so forth—all-pervading, reaching everywhere, and inexhaustible; Conformable, equal, and likewise true; Unattached, unbound, and equal to the Dharma-realm."
From this point, the second section clarifies that which is to be countered (*vipakṣa*).
This is divided into three parts:
first, the clarification of that which is to be countered; second, the differentiation of the arising of attachment; and third, the progressive superiority of what is cultivated.
Furthermore, first, to clarify that which is to be countered, the Sūtra states:
"By skillfully observing that the five aggregates, the three realms, and the two truths lack the characteristics of self or other, one attains their suchness."
The commentary states:

Regarding "skillfully observing the five aggregates" and so forth, this has already been explained previously. That is to say, by observing the five aggregates, one attains liberation from the aggregates; by observing the causes and effects of the three realms, one attains the patience of emptiness (*śūnyatā-ksānti*); and by observing the conventional and ultimate aspects of the two truths, one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-ksānti*).

"Absence of the marks of self and other" means observing that the aggregates and so forth do not abide at all; because there is neither subject nor object, and neither self nor other, there is no conceptual differentiation.
The text is further divided into three parts;
first, it clarifies the arising of the three realms.
Sūtra: "Although one constantly cultivates the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), one still takes birth within the three realms (*tridhātu*). Explanation:
"Although one constantly cultivates the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) and so forth" is an explanation that addresses a doubt and difficulty.
It means: since all the superior practices cultivated prior to this accord with the ultimate truth, what will they produce?

Although these practices are constantly cultivated as being in accord with the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), because they induce the segmented birth and death (*bhavāgra-cheda-jarāmaraṇa*) of the three realms, and because the seeds of habituation have not yet ceased and one has not yet abandoned the bonds of signs (*nimitta-bandhana*), the practices thus performed give rise to rebirth within the three realms.

The Sūtra speaks of the "three realms" (tridhātu) as a general characterization; however, for the most part, this refers only to the desire realm (kāmadhātu), as will be fully understood in due order.
Second, from here, the reason for this is investigated.
The Sūtra states:
"Why is this so? The commentary says:
This is an inquiry.
Third, this explains that which is produced.
The Sūtra says:
"Because the karmic habituation and its retribution have not yet been destroyed or exhausted, and because one is born in accordance with the Path among humans and devas."
The commentary states:
"Karmic habituation" refers to the cause;
"retribution" refers to the fruit.
Regarding "not yet destroyed": because the causes that induce birth have not been severed, birth in distinct segments has not yet been destroyed.
Regarding "among humans and devas": this is because only humans and devas of the desire realm receive superior births.
Why is it not the two higher realms, but only the humans and devas of the desire realm?
Because they possess direct realization (*abhisamaya*), and because this [state] is proximate to the first stage (*bhūmi*), whereas those two are not.
Regarding "birth in accordance with the path": it means that even after passing through successive births, one does not forget, due to the perfection of their nature.
What is clarified here is the lineage of those who proceed directly;
as for those who turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna], they have already been analyzed within the preceding discussion on the transformational body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
From this, thirdly, the practices to be cultivated are explained.
Sūtra: “One cultivates eighty-four thousand pāramitās of the superior grade. Commentary:
Regarding the stage above the Three Worthies, the remaining texts are exhaustive.
From here begins the third section, which concludes and applies the full stages.
This is divided into three parts:
Furthermore, first, to clarify the kalpas through which he passed, the Sūtra states:
"Throughout three asaṃkhyeya-kalpas, he cultivated the two types of beneficial practices, bringing about vast and extensive benefit."
The commentary states:
Regarding the "three asaṃkhyeya kalpas," this is because one additional kalpa is added to the preceding two.
It refers to the complete cultivation of the two benefits (self and others) for the sake of providing extensive and abundant aid.
From this, the second section clarifies the practice of renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*).
The Sūtra states:
"Having attained well-tamed samādhis, one dwells in superior discernment and cultivates the practice of renunciation."
The commentary states:
"Attaining excellent self-mastery" refers to having attained excellent self-mastery during the stage of the three levels of worthiness (*tri-śaikṣa*).
"Samādhi" is translated here as "equipoise" (*samāhita*), because one is constantly in association with the cultivation of various superior concentrations.

"Abiding in superior observation" refers to cultivating superior wisdom in its lower, middle, and upper grades, as well as for the purpose of inducing the practice of renunciation for the first bhūmi.

Furthermore, another interpretation holds that "cultivating the practices of the two benefits for the sake of vast and extensive benefit" clarifies that one primarily abides in external gates to cultivate bodhisattva practices during the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*); the subsequent passage beginning with "having attained thorough mastery" clarifies the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*).
The first two lines clarify the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) upon which [the practice] relies.
"Having attained thorough mastery" means that one has already attained the highest degree of mental mastery.
"All *samādhis*" refers to the concentrations that serve as the basis for the "attainment of clarity" (*vimalā-pratilambha*) and so forth.
These four are not identical, as they are termed the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*).
The following two lines clarify the stages of *ūṣmagata* and so forth.

Based on the four types of thorough investigation (*paryeṣaṇā*) and the four types of knowledge of reality as it is (*yathābhūtaparijñāna*), these are called superior observation (*viśeṣa-vipaśyanā*).

This brief explanation consists of three stages. First is the stage of "Heat" (*ūṣmagata*). Relying on the concentration of "attainment of clarity," one initiates the lower-level investigation and contemplates that there is nothing to be grasped as an object.

That is to say, within this stage, one initially contemplates the four factors—the name, the referent, the intrinsic nature, and the distinction of the object of apprehension—and realizes that these are all transformations of one's own mind, existing only as provisional designations, and that in reality they cannot be found.
Because it is the precursor to the initial attainment of the sun of wisdom, it is established as the stage named "Illumination" (*āloka*).
Furthermore, because it is the precursor to the fire of the Path thus attained, it is also called "Heat" (*uṣmagata*).

Second is the stage of the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*): relying on the concentration of increased illumination, one gives rise to superior investigation and contemplates the absence of anything to be grasped.

This means that within this stage, one repeatedly contemplates the four factors—namely, name and so forth—which are apprehended as objects; these are all transformations of one's own mind, existing only as provisional designations, and cannot be found in reality.
Because the characteristics of clarity become increasingly prominent, it is called "Increasing Clarity" (Vṛddhāloka).
Because it represents the ultimate limit of the stage of investigation (*vitarka*), it is further named "Summit" (*mūrdhan*).

Third is the stage of "Patience" (*kṣānti*): relying on the meditative concentration of sealing and conforming (*anuloma*), one generates the lower-level wisdom of reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) and correctly and universally knows the four dharmas—the names, meanings, self-natures, and distinctions. One definitively seals and maintains [the realization] that there is no object of apprehension (*grāhya*), and one also conforms to and accepts [the truth] within the absence of an apprehending subject (*grāhaka*). Since there is no real object apart from the apprehending consciousness, how could there be a real consciousness apart from the apprehended object?
Because it precedes the [Path of] Seeing and accords with what follows, it is established as the "Impression" (mudrā) and named accordingly;
because it endures the emptiness of the object, the consciousness, and the subject, it is also called "Patience" (kṣānti).

This is the fourth stage, the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma), which, relying on the Uninterrupted Samādhi (ānantarya-samādhi), gives rise to the superior, suchness-consistent wisdom that realizes the emptiness of the duality of grasper and grasped.

This means that while the preceding stage of "supreme patience" (kṣānti) only confirms the emptiness of the grasper, the present "highest mundane dharma" (laukikāgradharma) confirms both types of emptiness simultaneously; because one necessarily enters the path of seeing immediately thereafter, it is designated by the name "uninterrupted" (ānantarya).
Because this is the most supreme among all mundane dharmas (*laukika-dharma*), it is called the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*).

Likewise, in the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*) and Summits (*mūrdhan*), one contemplates the emptiness of the apprehended object based on the apprehending consciousness; when the lower stage of Patience (*kṣānti*) arises, one confirms the empty characteristic of the object;
and in the transition to the middle stage of Patience, one accords with and accepts that the apprehending consciousness is empty just as the object is.
At the stage where the highest patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) arises, one seals the emptiness of the grasper;
at the stage of the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), one seals both aspects of emptiness.
Because all of these still involve conceptual signs (*nimitta*), they have not yet realized the truth.

Therefore, the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* establishes this meaning, as a verse in that sūtra says: "When a bodhisattva is in the state of meditative concentration, they observe that reflections are nothing but mind.
Once the conceptualization of objects has been eliminated, they scrutinize that there is only one's own mental representation."
"Thus abiding in the internal mind, one knows that the apprehended does not exist; next, the apprehender is also absent; finally, one touches upon non-apprehension.

At this stage, the Bodhisattva practices the observation of both the established truths—the four [noble truths] such as suffering—and the unestablished truth, which is the single reality in its totality and the two types of emptiness in their particulars, in order to induce the two kinds of vision in the future.

When Bodhisattvas give rise to these roots of goodness, such as "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, although they may employ them during the stage of skillful means across all *dhyānas*, they attain fulfillment only by relying on the fourth *dhyāna*. Because one enters the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) by depending on this most excellent basis, [these roots] arise only in dependence upon a body within the happy migrations (*sugati*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Therefore, the *Xianyang lun* (Treatise on Manifesting the Doctrine), fascicle 16, states: "Extreme aversion does not pertain to the miserable realms (*apāya*), and extreme delight does not pertain to the two upper realms.
It occurs only among humans and devas of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) when a Buddha appears in the world and [they] realize direct insight (*abhisamaya*)."
All of the above constitutes abiding in superior observation (*viśeṣa-vipaśyanā*), because one cultivates the practices of renunciation that accord with the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, regarding the three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), the preceding section has entirely clarified the completion of the first eon.
The ancients established these four preparatory practices (*prayoga*) as follows:
the preparation for the first dhyāna is not subsumed under the desire realm, and the preparation for the first stage (*bhūmi*) is not subsumed within the first eon (*kalpa*).
One should raise this objection:

Regarding the statement that "the skillful means of the first stage are not [limited to] the first eon," the skillful means of the first stage are not subsumed under the category of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

If one were to say that they are not noble ones (*ārya*) because they have not yet realized the truth, then one should likewise say that they are not subsumed under the second eon because they have not yet realized the truth.
If one contemplates this text, there is no need to laboriously formulate objections.
This concludes the third section: the subsequent superior stage.
The Sūtra states:
"Because one is able to realize the stage of the noble ones (āryabhūmi) of equality.
The commentary explains:
"Being able to realize equality" means that distinct untainted wisdom (anāsravajñāna) directly realizes suchness (tathatā), and since suchness is precisely the stage of the noble ones of equality.
From here, the fourth [section] clarifies the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
This is divided into three parts:
first, the characteristics of entering the stage; second, the practice while abiding in the stage; and third, the conclusion that confirms the completion of the stage.
The initial section further consists of three parts;
first, the primary [part] marks the characteristics of entering the stages (*bhūmi*).
The Sūtra states:

"Furthermore, on the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva transcends the stage of ordinary beings (*bāla-bhūmi*), is born into the family of the Tathāgata, and dwells in the patience of equality (*samatā-kṣānti*).
The commentary states:

Regarding the auspicious signs that precede one’s ascent to the stages, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, chapter four, says: "The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Lion-Form Unobstructed Radiant Flame, saying:"

"Good son! This sign of the bodhisattva on the first stage first manifests as immeasurable and boundless various treasuries of jewels filling the trichiliocosm without exception, all of which the bodhisattva sees."
This is identical to the text on the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*) in the one hundred and fifteenth fascicle of the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, which constitutes the preceding signs.

As for the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), it refers to the initial realization of the supramundane mind; because one has attained what was previously unattained and now begins to attain it, supreme joy arises.
That which is called "ground" (bhūmi) has unconditioned virtues as its intrinsic nature, as explained previously.
Regarding the phrase "transcending the ground of fools": "fools" refers to ordinary, ignorant beings for whom ignorance serves as their ground.
Because one abandons those [defilements] through the untainted (*anāsrava*), it is called "transcending.

Regarding "being born into the family of the Tathāgata," the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* by Asvabhāva states: "The Buddha-dharmadhātu is called the 'family of the Tathāgata. Because one realizes and attains this, it is called 'birth'; for one is first born into the noble embryo (*āryagarbha*) and succeeds to the lineage of the Buddhas."

As stated in the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*: "Having transcended the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi*), one enters the rank of a bodhisattva, is born into the family of the Buddhas, and possesses a noble lineage."
Those who abide in the patience of equanimity truly have no high or low; hence it is called "equanimity.
When correct wisdom realizes the ultimate, this constitutes the patience of abiding.
From here, the second section clarifies the suchness that is realized.
Sūtra: "Initially, the wisdom of signlessness illuminates the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), which is the equality of the single characteristic—neither characterized nor signless. Commentary:

The first wisdom of signlessness refers to the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*); it is the non-conceptual wisdom that realizes the principle of the two kinds of emptiness. Because this stands at the very beginning, it is called the "first wisdom."
Although it is the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), in relation to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), it is considered the beginning; since this occurs prior to that, it is called "the first.
That which illuminates the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) does so because it realizes the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), which is the true ultimate revealed by the two kinds of emptiness.
Regarding "equality of the single characteristic": as wisdom is non-dual, it is the equality of the single characteristic.
Regarding "neither characteristic nor absence of characteristic": because there is no subject-object duality of characteristics, it is neither characteristic nor absence of characteristic.
From this, the third section clarifies the obstacles to be abandoned.
The Sūtra states:
"By severing all ignorance and extinguishing craving for the three realms, future immeasurable births and deaths shall never again arise."
The commentary states:
"Severing all ignorance" refers to that which arises from conceptual construction (*vikalpita*) within the two obstacles; since ignorance is not singular, it is termed "all.
Although only ignorance is mentioned, the grasping obstacles are all severed as well.
Ignorance is the root and the basis for the grasping hindrances; by severing ignorance alone, all others are severed accordingly, and thus it is singled out for mention.
"Extinguishing the greed of the three realms" refers to that which is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

This means that when the affliction of greed, together with ignorance, obstructs the increase of the perfection of generosity, it is because at the time of entering the first stage (*bhūmi*), the heavy residues (*dausthulya*) of greed are forever severed.

Regarding the phrase "because immeasurable future births and deaths will never arise again," this refers to the immeasurable births and deaths—such as those in the evil realms, the continent of Uttarakuru, and among the long-lived devas—which are brought about by the ten non-virtuous actions and various virtuous deeds produced by conceptual delusions; these will never arise again once one enters the first stage.
As stated in the fourth chapter of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, which eliminates two types of ignorance (*avidyā*):

first, the ignorance of clinging to the characteristics of self and phenomena; this refers to that which clings to characteristics within the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), taking duality as its basis because it speaks of "self" and "phenomena";
this is identical to what is here termed the elimination of all forms of ignorance.
Second is the fear of ignorance regarding the miserable destinies within the cycle of birth and death, which refers to the karmic fruits and so forth that lead to those miserable destinies;
this is equivalent to the immeasurable births and deaths of the future within this same context.

However, among these three, the former and latter are afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), while craving (*rāga*) is an affliction of cultivation (*bhāvanā-kleśa*); this is stated to show that all three types are to be abandoned forever.
As for the distinctions in their abandonment: first, ignorance (*avidyā*) is abandoned by its own nature;
next, craving for the three realms is abandoned through detachment (*visamyoga*) from the practice of giving (*dāna*), as its binding conditions are severed.
The causes and effects of immeasurable births and deaths are all non-existent, because they are neither produced nor annihilated.

The first two are cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and the latter is cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); the True Suchness (*tathatā*) thus realized is itself unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
From this point, the practice of the second stage (*bhūmi*) is divided into three parts:
first, the cultivation of compassion and wisdom; second, the investigation into whether wisdom is one or many; and third, the cultivation of wisdom and vows.
The first section clarifies compassion and wisdom; the text is divided into three parts:
first, a general presentation of compassion and wisdom; second, an explanation of the cultivation of sublime practices; and third, a differentiation of virtues according to the stages (*bhūmi*).
For now, we address the first part: the general presentation of compassion and wisdom.

Sūtra: “With great compassion as the foremost, they give rise to various great vows and, through the wisdom of skillful means, practice immeasurable superior deeds in every thought-moment. Explanation:
Great compassion is primary because it is the root of benefiting others.
The arousal of great vows is the basis for practice.
This is because practice and vows support one another like two sprouts; both must be cultivated together without partiality.
Regarding "knowledge of skillful means," this refers to the wisdom that penetrates conventional reality (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
As the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states: "With great compassion as the foremost and wisdom as predominant, it consists of all forms of knowledge subsumed by skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*)."

According to that sutra, this reveals that by relying on compassion and wisdom, one skillfully cultivates in every thought-moment the immeasurable, supreme practices for the benefit of oneself and others.
This is the second section, which clarifies the cultivation of these supreme practices.
The text is further divided into two parts;
first, the initial stage of practicing all the various deeds.
The Sūtra says:
"Neither realized nor unrealized, because one universally studies all [dharmas].
The commentary states:
"Non-realization" refers to the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*).
It is not that there is no realization, because it is a reflection.

According to the *Benji* (Original Record), it is said that there is no realization because the ultimate exists within the conventional; yet it is not that there is no realization because the conventional exists within the ultimate.

Regarding the "Universal Learner" (sarvatra-śaikṣa): they dwell within this stage for one incalculable eon (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), because they universally cultivate and learn the myriad practices (*sādhana*) as their adornment.
This is as explained at length in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, which states that through extensively studying diverse doctrines, one comes to universally know the underlying intent (*abhiprāya*).
This is because, as stated in the *Śīla-sūtra*, one must study all the treatises of the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*).
Furthermore, this practice is explained in detail in the thirty-fourth chapter of the *Samantabhadra-caryā-praṇidhāna* and in the second and third sections of the *Daśabhūmika-bhāṣya*.
From this, the second [point] is "heading toward omniscience.
The Sūtra says:
"Neither abiding nor not abiding, because one is heading toward omniscience."
The commentary states:
"Not abiding" means that while universally practicing all deeds, one does not dwell in cessation.
"Not non-abiding" means that regarding the practices being cultivated, the mind is without distraction, remaining constantly in tranquility.
Because one who is directed toward the Omniscient One enters into all-encompassing wisdom through every practice and vow they cultivate.
From this, the third section distinguishes the virtues based on the stages (*bhūmi*).
This is divided into four parts:
Furthermore, at the outset, the first Māra was unable to move him.
As the Sūtra says:
"Because Māra cannot move one who courses through birth and death."
The commentary states:
"To act within birth and death" refers to the sphere where one benefits sentient beings.

"That Māras cannot move them" refers to the four Māras—namely, the Māra of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*), the Māra of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*), the Māra of death (*mṛtyu-māra*), and the celestial Māra (*devaputra-māra*)—as was already extensively analyzed above in the "Introductory Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*).

As stated in the first fascicle of the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*: "From the first bhūmi upward, the great bodhisattvas, dwelling within the pure lands, are free from the four coarse māras and possess no fivefold fears."
From this point on is the second [section], "Free from All Fears.
The Sūtra states:
"Because one is free from 'I' and 'mine,' there is no fear."
The commentary states:
"One who is free from 'I' and 'mine' has permanently severed that which arises from conceptual discrimination.
There are five kinds of fearlessness:"

First, the fear of lacking a livelihood; second, the fear of ill repute; third, the fear of death; fourth, the fear of the evil realms; and fifth, the fear of being intimidated by the majesty of the great assembly.
Regarding the analysis of the basis for these five, the second fascicle of the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "These five fears are obstacles to the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*)."
The first two and the fifth depend on body, speech, and mind; the third and fourth depend on the body, because the body differs according to whether it is characterized by attachment or aversion.
Regarding the analysis of the five causes, there are briefly two types:
the first is false cognition that grasps erroneously due to conceptualization, views, and craving.
Second, because their roots of goodness are slight.

Regarding that which can act as an antidote, the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* and the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* state: "Because this bodhisattva is free from the notion of a self, he does not even cherish his own body, let alone material wealth."
He has no fear of being unable to support himself, for he does not seek offerings from others but is solely dedicated to providing for all sentient beings;
he has no fear of ill repute, for he is far removed from the view of self and possesses no notion of a self; and he has no fear of death.
Knowing for myself that after death I shall certainly not be separated from the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, I have no fear of the evil realms.
My aspirations and joys are such that none in all the world can equal them, let alone surpass them.
"Because there is no fear regarding the majesty and virtue of the great assembly.
This summarizes the state of being without dread.
From this point, the third [section] concerns the constant transformation of sentient beings.
Sūtra: "There is no distinction between self and other, because one constantly transforms sentient beings. Commentary:
Regarding "being without the marks of self or other," this means attaining non-discrimination because one does not dwell upon marks.

Regarding "constantly transforming sentient beings," as the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states: "Furthermore, one makes a great vow: 'May all those bound within the three realms, entering the six destinies and comprised by name-and-form in all such classes of birth—may I transform them all to lead them into the Buddha-dharma, causing them to forever sever all worldly destinies and establish them in the path of omniscience, without ceasing until the end of the future.'"
Therefore, he has been constantly transforming beings ever since.
From this fourth [birth], he has been born in various pure lands. Sūtra:
"Because through the power of sovereign vows, one is born in all pure lands.
The commentary states:
"The power of sovereign vows" means that vows attain sovereignty by virtue of the power of practice.
Those who are born in the various pure lands do so because these are the lands of enjoyment for all Buddhas.
Nevertheless, the self-enjoyment land of this Bodhisattva is no different in location from the lands of the Buddhas; however, their essential natures are distinct as previously described.
What is the nature and form of this land of enjoyment (*sambhogakāya-kṣetra*), and by what vehicle or path is one born there?

As stated in the first fascicle of the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra*: "The pure lands of all Buddhas are circular and boundless; their measure is difficult to fathom. They transcend the spheres traversed within the triple world (*tridhātu*) and are produced by supramundane roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). Their characteristic is the most supreme mastery of pure consciousness (*viśuddha-vijñāna*)."

As the Tathāgata beholds this assembly of great bodhisattvas gathered like clouds, they take great mindfulness, wisdom, and conduct as their path for wandering; great tranquility and sublime insight as their vehicle; and the liberations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness as their gateways of entry.

The aforementioned sutra spoke of cultivating the three gates of liberation; here, it further speaks of the power of sovereign vows. This reveals that vows attain sovereignty through practice, and that one is born by relying upon the path of that vehicle.
How is it known that these are born in those respective lands?
That treatise explains: "Because Bodhisattvas on the [Bodhisattva] stages are born in the Land of Enjoyment for Others.
From this, secondly, the identity or difference of the wisdoms is clarified.
This section is divided into three parts;
first, the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is elucidated. Sūtra:
“Good son! This initial awakening-wisdom is neither like-ness nor wisdom; it is neither existent nor non-existent, and lacks two characteristics. Explanation:
This "initial awakening wisdom" refers to the wisdom of entering the stages (*bhūmi*).
"Awakening" means awakening-illumination, which is the wisdom that realizes reality (*tattva*).
It is "neither like [the object] nor like wisdom" because both the objective realm and wisdom are empty.
"Neither existent nor non-existent" means that both existence and non-existence are quiescent.
"There are no two characteristics" means that both subject and object have perished.
This refers to the observation of equality by the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, as these two categories of wisdom first arise therein.
From this, the second section clarifies the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*).
The Sūtra says:
"The wondrous function of skillful means is neither inverted nor abiding, neither moving nor still."
The commentary states:
"The wondrous function of skillful means" refers to the wisdom that penetrates conventional reality; it is called a "wondrous function" because its essence is endowed with the four virtues.
"Not inverted" means that although it involves the perception of signs, it is not erroneous.
It is not abiding, because it cultivates all myriad practices rather than abiding in any one.
It is not moving, because it contemplates preceding objects through suchness-wisdom without distraction or agitation.
It is not still, because it rides upon great wisdom and compassion to cultivate non-abiding.

Furthermore, the first [point] distinguishes [the Buddha] from non-Buddhists; the second distinguishes him from ordinary devas; and the two aspects of movement and stillness distinguish him from the Two Vehicles, because they lack this wisdom and thus do not share it.
From this follows the third point: the identity and difference of the two types of wisdom.

Sūtra: "The mastery of the two benefits is like water and its waves, which are neither identical nor different; likewise, the arising of wisdom and the various pāramitās are neither identical nor different. Explanation:

Regarding "mastery over the two benefits": true wisdom constitutes self-benefit, while skillful means constitute the stage of benefiting others; one possesses mastery over the functioning of these two benefits.
The phrase "like water and waves" provides an analogy to explain and establish this point.
Water is a metaphor for fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and waves are a metaphor for subsequent wisdom (*prṣṭha-labdha-jñāna*); the functions of these two are like those of waves and water.

They are neither identical nor different: they are not identical because their movement and stillness differ, yet they are not different because there are no waves apart from water; this is precisely the meaning of the non-identity and non-difference of these two wisdoms.

That the arising of the various *pāramitās* from wisdom is neither identical nor different means that one practices based on wisdom, such that the practice and the wisdom coexist, just as waves and water are neither identical nor different.
From here, the third section clarifies the cultivation of wisdom and vows.
This is divided into two parts;
first, it clarifies the practice to be cultivated.
Sūtra: “Over the course of four asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he fully cultivated and perfected ten million koṭis of practices and vows. Commentary:
Regarding the "four asaṃkhyeyas," this is because one kalpa is added to the aforementioned three.

As for the phrase "cultivation and so forth," regarding the distinction between this practice and that of the *śaikṣa* (the stage of the worthy), according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*: "The first asaṃkhyeya kalpa is called *pāramitā*, because within a single practice one cultivates a single practice."
The second incalculable eon is named "Approaching the Perfections" (*upaparamitā*), because within a single practice one cultivates all practices.
The third incalculable eon is named "Great Perfections" (*mahāparamitā*), because within all practices one cultivates all practices.

Since the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, chapter four, and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, chapter nine, also state this, the present stage of cultivation corresponds to the second eon; thus, it differs from the stage of the "Worthy One" (*bhadra*).
Next is the second [power], the power of wisdom and aspiration.
The Sūtra states:

"The Bodhisattvas on this stage have no karmic habit-energies of the three realms and do not create any new karma, because they take birth through the power of their aspirations in accordance with the power of their wisdom."
The commentary states:

Regarding "those who lack the karmic habit-energies of the three realms," *karma* refers to volitional action (*saṃskāra*), while *habit-energy* (*vāsanā*) refers to the latencies; this encompasses both seeds and manifest states.
This is because those [defilements] abandoned through seeing have already been eliminated.

Regarding "no longer creating new [karma]": when ignorance that deludes one regarding the principle (li) gives rise to new karma through its activity, since that has already been severed, one no longer creates new karma.
From this point onward, up until the tenth stage (bhūmi), the practices and vows cultivated do not produce further rebirth, because the ignorance that first entered the stages has been severed.
If that is so, what distinguishes the ignorance (*avidyā*) of subsequent stages from that of the preceding one?
Furthermore, when Bodhisattvas on the stages manifest greed, anger, and so forth, are these not karma? Answer:
Furthermore, subsequent ignorance consists solely of innate afflictions; although there are instances where it does not arise, it does not incite karma.

Moreover, because the sentient beings to be converted by Bodhisattvas possess diverse dispositions and inclinations such that their conditions for conversion vary, they manifest greed and anger through the power of great compassion.

As in the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra, chapter sixty-eight, and in the cases of the woman Vāsukī and King Anantayaśas in chapter sixty-six, each attained immeasurable samādhis; how could it be that they were the same as those seen [in other contexts] who are unwholesome?
If that were so, then those superior retributions on the stages would have no cause.

This is not the case, because they take the accumulation of provisions (*sambhāra*) and other stages prior to the [first] stage as their cause, with ignorance-initiated activity (*avidyā-pravṛtti*) serving as the causal condition.
Regarding the statement "because they take birth through vows in accordance with their power of wisdom," the masters of the Western regions (India) have two interpretations. Some say:

those who attain gradual enlightenment and those whose wisdom predominates have permanently severed the continuity of afflictions that produce and moisten rebirth; thus, within the three realms, they no longer undergo birth in discrete segments (*bhavāgra*). Instead, the retribution of the ten kings is received as a transformation-rebirth (*nirmāṇakāya*) through the power of vows associated with untainted meditative concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*), in accordance with their power of wisdom.
It is not so, for those ten kings would otherwise not exist there.
Furthermore, if those born outside the realm were not within the sphere of ordinary perception, then the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas would likewise not perceive them. Some say:
There was a master of the Abhidharma named Vinayaprabha who, relying on the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, spoke as follows:

"A certain class of those who attain sudden enlightenment and for whom compassion is predominant possesses, prior to the [bodhisattva] stages, the causes for the attainment of a superior body through cultivation; they retain the seeds of the afflictions associated with remaining phenomena, which are moistened by the power of their wisdom and vows to bring about that birth."

From the eighth stage upward, birth is exclusively through transformation; they can be seen in both concentrated and non-concentrated states. Therefore, prior to the seventh stage, such as the fruit of the ten kings, all are born in a real sense.
From this, the third section concludes the *Bhūmi* (Stage).
The Sūtra states:

"In every thought-moment, one constantly practices the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*); through generosity, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation, one is vast and pure, and is well able to abide in benefiting sentient beings. The commentary explains:

Regarding "one who constantly practices in every thought-moment": among the ten perfections, the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) is preeminent, because one practices the fulfillment of material gifts, the Dharma, and fearlessness; yet it is not that the others are not practiced, for they are cultivated according to one's capacity and circumstances.
Regarding "generosity and so forth," this is because their extensive cultivation is entirely pure.

As stated in the *Daśabhūmika-bhāṣya*, which differs slightly from this [text], its third section says: "One gathers sentient beings by means of two methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), namely: generosity and kind speech."
The latter two inclusions rely solely on the power of faith and understanding; their practice has not yet reached full penetration.
"Skillfully abiding in equanimity" and so forth conclude the section on perfection.
From here begins the fifth stage, the Stainless Ground (*vimalā-bhūmi*).
The textual structure has three parts as before; first, the initial section marks the characteristics of entering the stages (*bhūmi*).
The Sūtra says:

"Furthermore, in the Stainless Stage (*vimalā-bhūmi*), the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*) are supremely quiescent, severing the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of anger and so forth."
The commentary states:

Regarding the clarification of entering the stages (*bhūmi*), the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* says: "For a Bodhisattva of the second stage, this sign appears beforehand: the great trichiliocosm is as level as the palm of a hand, and the Bodhisattva sees all its various wondrous colors and pure, precious ornaments, which are immeasurable and boundless."
Regarding the "Stainless Ground" (*vimalā-bhūmi*): because all subtle stains, transgressions, and faults of impaired morality have become completely purified, it is called "Stainless.

Regarding the "four immeasurables" (*catvāry apramāṇāni*): because one has severed the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of anger and so forth on this ground, the four immeasurables arise in association with the mind that enters this stage.
The "supremely quiescent" refers to the *tathatā* (suchness) that has been realized.
This corresponds to the realization of supreme *tathatā* as described in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, which states that it is so called because it is endowed with boundless, supreme qualities.
"Severing the habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of anger and so forth" clarifies that which is to be severed.
"Habit-energy" refers to *vāsanā*, which has two meanings:
first, the seeds of afflictions such as anger; second, the coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*) and lack of functional capacity (*akarmanyatā*) conditioned by anger and so forth.
"Equal" also has two meanings:
first, it is equal to those secondary afflictions such as anger, malice, and harm; second, it is equal to the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that accompany them.
Regarding the ignorance (*avidyā*) to be abandoned, there are furthermore two types.
As stated in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*: "First is the ignorance of erring in the subtle precepts, which is a portion co-arising with this stage;
second is the ignorance that initiates various karmic actions, which refers to the three types of karma resulting from those errors."
"These [factors] such as ignorance all obstruct the utterly pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) of the second stage; because they are forever abandoned upon entering the second stage.

Regarding the distinction of abandonment: these associated factors such as anger abandon only the *dauṣṭhulya* (coarseness) and the lack of functional capacity (*akarmanyatā*), but do not abandon the seeds.
Since seeds such as anger are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),

the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only), chapter ten, states that they are gradually suppressed prior to the stages of cultivation, and from the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) upward, they can be suddenly and completely suppressed so that they never again manifest.
Although these may temporarily manifest during the first seven stages, they do not constitute a fault; from the eighth stage upward, they are never again practiced.
Within the ten stages, their seeds are not severed individually; rather, at the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), all are severed instantaneously.
Question:
These two categories—the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and the coarse habitual tendencies of anger (*dveṣadauṣṭhulya*)—are distinct; are they both abandoned simultaneously? Answer:

Regarding what is abandoned by insight (*vipaśyanā*): although the two categories differ, it is not the case that a separate, uninterrupted, and coarse heavy-laden state (*dausthulya*) of anger arises apart from the obstacles themselves.
Since beginningless time, this has coexisted with the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), which serves as its root; thus, the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*) abandons this root obstacle.
Because the heavy nature of hatred and the heavy nature of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are both abandoned simultaneously within the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).

As for the difference in the timing of their abandonment: when the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*) arises, the seeds of the obscurations have already ceased to exist, yet that state of unfitness (*akarmanyatā*) has not yet been abandoned.
In order to abandon this [unfitness], the path of liberation arises.

The arising of the path of liberation is not solely for this purpose, but also for the realization of the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) belonging to this category.
Thus, the state of unfitness perishes simultaneously with the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), while the attainment of the unconditioned arises simultaneously with the path of liberation.

Regarding the two obstacles severed within the ten stages—the severance of their seeds and their residual habits, as well as the paths of uninterrupted continuity and liberation that effect this severance—all such matters are to be understood by analogy with this.
Following this is the second section: the cultivation of the stages.
This section is divided into two parts;
first, the cultivation of the ten wholesome actions.
The Sūtra states:

"Cultivate all practices, namely: staying far removed from killing and taking what is not given; having a mind free from defiled desire; attaining truthful speech, harmonious speech, gentle speech, and disciplined speech; constantly practicing equanimity, constantly giving rise to a mind of loving-kindness, and abiding in an upright mind."
The commentary states:
"Practicing all deeds" is the general heading.
The following section clarifies the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*).
The first three bodily actions consist of abstaining from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.
The subsequent four verbal actions consist of distancing oneself from false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous chatter.
The latter three refer to mental karma, because they are free from the unwholesome roots of greed, hatred, and delusion.

This means that this bodhisattva’s perfection of the *pāramitā* of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) is complete, and their three types of action are pure, as they are endowed with the ten wholesome paths of action.
Regarding the analysis of its nature: according to our own school (Vaibhāṣika), it consists of seven types of matter and three mental factors.

According to the Sautrāntika, it is merely volition (cetanā), because it comprises three functions: moving the body, initiating speech, and the activities of deliberation, determination, and execution.
The Mahāyāna also considers this, as even the provisional is form.

To distinguish the differences, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle four, states: "By accumulating the causes and conditions of the ten paths of wholesome action, one is born among humans up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*)."

Furthermore, when these superior ten paths of wholesome action are practiced in conjunction with the contemplation of wisdom, because the mind is narrow and inferior, because one feels weary of and fears the triple world, because one is remote from great compassion, and because one attains understanding through hearing the voice of another, they constitute the Śrāvaka vehicle.

Furthermore, when these superior ten paths of wholesome action are cultivated and purified—because one awakens through self-insight rather than the instruction of another, because one lacks the full equipment of great compassion and skillful means, yet because one has realized the profound law of dependent origination—one accomplishes the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddha.

Furthermore, when these superior paths of ten wholesome actions are cultivated to purity—because the mind is immeasurably vast, because they are endowed with compassion, because they are embraced by skillful means, because they give rise to great vows, because they do not abandon sentient beings, because they seek the great wisdom of all Buddhas, because they purify the various stages of a bodhisattva, and because they purely cultivate all the perfections—they constitute the vast conduct of a bodhisattva.

Furthermore, these progressively superior ten paths of wholesome action are so because they are pure in every respect, because they realize the ten powers, because they realize the four fearlessnesses, and because all Buddha-dharmas are thereby accomplished.
This clearly explains that all realms of existence, all vehicles, and even the fruit of Buddhahood arise from the ten wholesome actions, as they possess these distinct differences.

Regarding the three types of ripened results (*vipāka-phala*) that correspond to the opposite—the ten unwholesome actions—that sutra continues: "The superior path of the ten unwholesome karmas is the cause for rebirth in hell; the middling is the cause for rebirth as an animal; and the inferior is the cause for rebirth as a hungry ghost. It is because of this that one is born into the three evil destinies."
Regarding the fruit of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*): if one is born among humans, there are two fruits for killing:

a short lifespan and much illness. For stealing, there are two fruits: [The text continues: ...a short lifespan and much illness. For stealing, there are two fruits: [the rest of the sentence follows].
Poverty leads to the loss of wealth and a lack of autonomy.
Sexual misconduct has two fruits:
one's wife will not be chaste and virtuous, and one will not obtain a retinue according to one's wishes.
The two fruits of false speech are:
being frequently slandered and being deceived by others.
The two fruits of divisive speech are:
The two fruits of coarse and evil [karma] are: one's retinue becomes estranged and one's kinsmen are wicked;
one constantly hears foul sounds and one's speech is full of strife and litigation.
The two fruits of impurity:
speaking as if no one were listening and speech that is not clear.
The two fruits of covetousness:
The mind is never satisfied and its desires are insatiable.
Hatred has two fruits:
one is being constantly sought out by others for one's faults, and the other is being perpetually tormented and harmed by others.
Wrong view has two fruits:
being born into a family of wrong views and having a mind that is deceitful and crooked;
these are its results of natural homogeneity (*niṣyanda-phala*) among human beings.

Regarding the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*), as the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "The body lacks luster and constantly encounters frost and hail; the body is covered in much dust and grime, and the mouth is perpetually foul-smelling."
"The seasons change with much uncertainty; dwellings are perilous and winding, resulting in few external fruits.
Fruits are mostly pungent, or else they are few or non-existent.
This refers to the predominant results (adhipati-phala) among human beings.
That sutra concludes: "The ten unwholesome paths can give rise to these immeasurable and boundless masses of great suffering; therefore, one should distance oneself from them.
One should take the ten wholesome paths as the garden of the Dharma, constantly abiding therein oneself and likewise exhorting others to do so."
From this follows the second practice for abandoning faults.
The Sūtra says:
"Tranquil and purely virtuous, free from the defilement of breaking the precepts, one practices the contemplation of great compassion so that it manifests in every thought-moment."
The commentary states:
"Tranquil and purely wholesome" means that the three karmas are tranquil because they are free from clamor and agitation.
"Ten wholesome paths without admixture" refers to their being purely wholesome.
"Free from the defilement of broken precepts" means that one's conduct is pure.
"Practicing the contemplation of great compassion" means that one has attained supreme meditative concentration.
"Manifesting before one in every thought-moment" means that there is no interruption.
From this, the third section concludes the *Pūrṇabhūmi*.
The Sūtra states:
"Throughout five asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he fully perfected the pāramitā of pure ethical discipline; his resolve was courageous and vigorous, and he was forever free from all defilements."
The commentary states:
Regarding the "five asaṃkhyeyas," this is because one kalpa is added to the preceding four.
As for "complete" and so forth, it means that the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā) increases predominantly, while the others increase according to their respective proportions.
One whose will and intention are courageous acts without retreat;
one who is forever free from all defilements is pure and perfect.
From this, the sixth stage, the Luminous Ground (*prabhākari-bhūmi*), is elucidated.
The textual structure has three parts as before; first, the initial section marks the characteristics of entering the stage.
The Sūtra says:
"Furthermore, in the Radiant Stage (*prabhākari-bhūmi*), the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva abides in non-conceptualization and extinguishes the darkness of ignorance."
The commentary states:

Regarding the clarification of entering the stages (*bhūmi*), the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* says: "For a Bodhisattva of the third stage, this sign first appears: his own body is courageous, strong, and adorned with armor; he is able to subdue all enemies and thieves, and the Bodhisattva perceives them all."

Regarding the Ground of Radiance (*Prabhākārī-bhūmi*): because its immeasurable wisdom and the light of samādhi are unshakable and cannot be overcome by any, and because it takes the dhāraṇī of hearing and retaining as its foundation, it is named the Ground of Radiance.
"Dwelling in non-conceptualization" refers to the very entry into the non-conceptual wisdom of the [first] stage (*bhūmi*).
This clarifies that the wisdom which realizes must necessarily have an object of realization, namely *tathatā* (suchness).

According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the Bodhisattva on this stage realizes the "superiorly flowing" *tathatā*; this means that the teachings flowing forth from this *tathatā* are far superior to all other teachings.
This means that by means of the three types of wisdom attained through this stage, one illuminates the Mahāyāna Dharma and realizes the fundamental *tathatā* (suchness) of these teachings.
"Extinguishing the darkness of ignorance" clarifies the severing of hindrances; it refers to entering this stage and abandoning the hindrance of dullness and darkness.

A portion of the innate cognitive obstructions (jñeyāvaraṇa) obstructs the superior meditative concentrations and dhāraṇīs of those three stages, as well as the three types of sublime wisdom (prajñā) they produce.
As stated in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, there are two kinds of ignorance:
first, the ignorance of craving for what has not yet been attained but is now being attained; this refers to that which obstructs superior concentration and cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
"Attachment" refers to affliction; it coexists with ignorance, and together they are able to act as obstacles.
These two are able to obstruct the superior dhāraṇī of ignorance, meaning they obstruct the dhāraṇī of the wisdoms of hearing and reflection.
In Sanskrit it is called *dhāraṇī*, which here is translated as "total retention" (*zongchi*); its essence consists of mindfulness and wisdom.
According to the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*, there are four kinds:
first, the retention of dharmas, which retains names, phrases, and syllables.
Second is the retention of meaning (*arthadhāraṇī*), which retains the meanings expressed;
third is the analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*); and fourth is uninterrupted eloquence (*pratibhāna*).
Because one has attained the wisdom of patience (*kṣānti-jñāna*), one does not forget these four types of retention.

In this stage, one seeks the Dharma with tireless diligence; as the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle five, states: "Even if the great trichiliocosm were filled with raging flames, one would cast oneself directly into them in order to seek a single phrase of the Dharma taught by the Buddha."
From this point, there is the practice of the second stage (bhūmi).
This is divided into three parts;
first, the initial section demonstrates the attainment of the three types of supernormal knowledge (vidyā).

Sūtra: “One attains the three insights (trividyā) within the patience of signlessness (animitta-kṣānti), fully knowing that throughout the three periods of time there is neither coming nor going. Explanation:
Regarding the patience of signlessness (*animitta-kṣānti*): wisdom that takes signlessness as its object is called the patience of signlessness.

As for attaining the three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*): first, the clear knowledge of recollecting past abodes; second, the clear knowledge of death and rebirth; and third, the clear knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya-vidyā*). These are explained in detail as previously described.

To know fully that the three periods of time have neither coming nor going means that, by means of these three types of supernormal knowledge (*vidyā*), one first knows the past, next knows the future, and finally knows the present; having thoroughly understood the three periods of time and realized their essence to be empty, there is no coming or going.
From this, secondly, the meditative concentrations to be cultivated are explained.
The Sūtra states:
"Based on the four dhyānas and the four formless absorptions, non-conceptual wisdom follows in successive order."
The commentary states:
Regarding "based on the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments," the dhyānas and formless attainments have already been explained above.
These two types of meditative concentration consist of eight distinct stages.

Regarding these distinctions: each of the first seven [stages] has three types—pure (*śuddha*), with relish (*āsvādana*), and untainted (*anāsrava*)—due to the distinction between ordinary beings and noble ones;
the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) has only two, because it lacks the untainted.
Non-conceptual wisdom refers to that which is entirely free from conceptualization during the stages of preparation (*prayoga*), the fundamental (*maula*), and subsequent attainment (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*).
Wisdom that accords with the sequence refers to the wisdom of subsequent attainment.
How is this known to be so?
It is because preparatory wisdom (prayoga-jñāna) induces fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna), and the category of fundamental wisdom realizes ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
Furthermore, based on the various practices of subsequently attained wisdom (pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna), one cultivates all [perfections] upon reaching the eighth stage (aṣṭamī-bhūmi).
"Conformity" (anuloma) refers to the sense of cultivation; it means proceeding from the lower stages to the upper ones in a conforming manner of entry.
This is as described in the twenty-eighth fascicle of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* regarding the cultivation of the "leap-over" meditative attainments (*vyutkrāntakasamāpatti*).

The verse of that treatise states: "The two types of meditative attainments proceed in both direct and reverse order, with equal intervals and sequential progression; furthermore, by skipping to the interval and skipping across, they are perfected.
Regarding the division of the fundamental wholesome attainments (*samāpatti*) of the preceding eight stages, there are two types:
first, those with outflows (*sāsrava*), and second, those without outflows (*anāsrava*).
Ascending is called "conformity" (ānulomika); descending back down is called "contrariety" (pratiloma).
Being of the same category is called "uniform" (sama); being of different categories is called "intermediate" (vyavakīrṇa).
Being adjacent is called "sequential" (anukrama); skipping one [stage] is called "leaping" (utkramya).

Regarding "reaching the leap-over as completion": this refers to when a practitioner cultivates the leap-over concentration (*vyutkrāntaka-samādhi*), they repeatedly practice by manifesting the eight contaminated stages (*sāsrava-bhūmi*) in both forward and reverse order;
the seven uncontaminated stages (*anāsrava-bhūmi*) in both forward and reverse order;

and the contaminated and uncontaminated stages in alternating forward and reverse order. When they repeatedly practice by leaping over the contaminated stages in both forward and reverse order, and leaping over the uncontaminated stages in both forward and reverse order, this is called the fulfillment of the preparatory application (*prayoga-paripūri*).

The attainment of the untainted meditative absorptions (*anāsrava-samāpatti*) through alternating forward and reverse progression is called the accomplishment of the "leap-over" concentration (*vyutkrāntaka-samādhi*).

This corresponds to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s Lion-Yawn Samādhi (*siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*) and the Gathering-and-Dispersing Samādhi (*saṃcayavyaya-samādhi*) in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, which will be fully explained below.

As the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "For what reason does a bodhisattva on this stage enter the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*)?
It is for the sake of five kinds of sentient beings."

First, for the sake of entering the various dhyānas for those sentient beings who are arrogant due to the pleasure of meditative concentration; second, for the sake of entering the formless absorptions for those sentient beings who are arrogant regarding the formless liberations; third, for the sake of causing suffering and distressed sentient beings to dwell securely in wholesome states and be granted eternal happiness, to resolve their suffering so they shall not undergo it, and to enter the various dhyāna-concentrations to give rise to immeasurable loving-kindness and compassion; fourth, for the sake of entering the immeasurables of sympathetic joy and equanimity for those sentient beings who have already attained liberation; fifth, for the sake of entering superior supernormal powers to inspire correct faith in those sentient beings who rely on false refuges.

Because one attains non-retrogressive dhyāna on this stage, it is called the "Stage of Samādhi" (*samādhī-bhūmi*); it is not that the preceding stage lacks this quality, but rather that this stage is superior.
Among these five [topics], the first four gates belong to this section, while the fifth, supernatural power (*abhijñā*), belongs to the subsequent section.
From this, the third section clarifies the attainment of the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
This is divided into two parts;
first, the initial section provides a general outline of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and so forth.
Sūtra: "Being fully endowed with supreme concentration, one attains the five supernormal powers. Explanation:
"One who is fully endowed with supreme meditative concentration" refers to the first eight dhyānas.
Among these, the first four serve as the basis for the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
"One who has attained the five supernormal powers" is the general designation for such a person.
From here, the second section specifically clarifies the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

The Sūtra says: "He manifests his body in various sizes with mastery over concealment and appearance; with the pure divine eye, he perceives all realms of existence; with the pure divine ear, he hears all sounds; with the knowledge of others' minds, he knows the thoughts of sentient beings; and through the recollection of past lives, he can know their infinite varieties."
The commentary states:
Among these five, the objects of the first, third, and fourth [knowledges] exist only in the present, because that which is manifested and known through hearing is exclusively of the present.
As for the "boundaries of the objects," it is as stated in the aforementioned sutra: "ten thousand Buddha-fields."

Fifth is the knowledge of the past; as the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states: "One recollects and knows the past immeasurable hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, billions, and trillions of nayutas of kalpas exactly as they were."
The second [knowledge] is the knowledge of the future; its meaning should be understood in full by analogy with that of the past.

Furthermore, regarding the "clear vision" (*vidarśanā*) mentioned in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, the first four [knowledges] are clear wisdom (*vidyā*), while the fifth is clear vision (*vidarśanā*).

However, the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* enumerates five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*): first, the power of supernatural faculties; second, the power of the divine ear; third, the power of knowing others' minds; fourth, the power of recollecting past lives; and fifth, the power of the divine eye.
Based on this sequence, the wise see the distinctions; it is not otherwise.

Regarding the differences among the three types of karma, that treatise states next: "The first supernormal power is the purity of bodily karma; the divine ear and knowledge of others' minds are the purity of vocal karma; and the recollection of past lives and knowledge of death and rebirth are the purity of mental karma."

Regarding the difference in the objects of knowledge: first, the supernormal power of psychic travel (*ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna*) differs because it can reach the abodes of sentient beings through the excellence of bodily transport, resolve, or mental speed;
the supernormal power of the divine ear (*divya-śrotra-jñāna*) differs because it can know the meaning of the sounds of the Dharma being preached;

and the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others (*paracitta-jñāna*) differs because it can fully comprehend all verbal expressions and teach according to the various names used by sentient beings based on those meanings.
The two supernormal knowledges of past and future exist because they fully know the past and future circumstances through which sentient beings should be transformed.
Their definitions and essential natures are as explained in the "Introduction Chapter" (Āmaṇasikāra-parivarta).
From here, the third section concludes the *Pūrṇabhūmi*.
The Sūtra states:
"Throughout six asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he practiced all the pāramitās of patience, attained the great dhāraṇī, and brought benefit and peace to others."
The commentary states:
Regarding the "six asaṃkhyeyas," they are added as previously described.

As for the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), this [perfection] increases preeminently; it does not mean that the others are not cultivated, for they are practiced according to one's capacity.
"Attaining great dhāraṇī" means that the four kinds [of dhāraṇī] are fully perfected as previously described.
"Benefiting and bringing peace and happiness" refers to the culmination of altruistic activity.
From this follows the seventh stage, the Radiant Wisdom (Arciṣmatī-bhūmi).
The textual structure has three parts as before; first, the initial section marks the characteristics of entering the stage.
The Sūtra says:

"Furthermore, in the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (Arciṣmatī-bhūmi), the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the conforming patience (anulomikī-kṣānti), remaining without grasping, because he has forever severed the subtle views of self and body (satkāya-dṛṣṭi)."
The commentary states:

To clarify the entry into the stages (*bhūmi*), the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* says: "For a Bodhisattva of the fourth stage, these signs appear beforehand: wind-circles from the four directions scatter and spread all manner of wondrous flowers across the ground, which the Bodhisattva perceives in their entirety."

The Ground of Blazing Wisdom (Arciṣmatī-bhūmi) is so called because one burns away all afflictions with the fire of wisdom and increases the light by cultivating the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma).
"Practicing compliant patience" refers to the lower grade of the third stage of compliant patience (anulomikī-kṣānti).
"Cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) refers to repeated practice; "practice" (*caryā*) refers to progressive advancement.

Although the term "patience" (*kṣānti*) is used generally, the wisdom that enables one to enter this stage and realize the truth is called "conformable patience" (*anulomikī-kṣānti*), because the sense of "patience" is predominant at the moment of first realizing this principle.
That which is without anything grasped is the suchness that is realized.
This means that this true suchness has no point of attachment; it is not attached to a self, because it is not that upon which the grasping of a self and so forth depends.
"Because of the permanent severance of subtle views of self and what belongs to self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)" refers to the obstacles that are abandoned.
This refers to the views of self and what belongs to self among the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) that are associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

They are called "subtle" because these views of self and what belongs to self are of the lowest grade, because they do not function as objects of deliberate attention (*amanasikāra*), and because they persistently follow along with active manifestation; for these reasons, they are designated as "subtle."
Because those [afflictions] obstruct the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) of this stage, they are permanently severed upon entering this stage.
Ignorance associated with [wrong] views constitutes the cognitive obscuration (jñeyāvaraṇa), and this is of two kinds.
As stated in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*:

"The first is the ignorance of attachment to the joy of meditative absorption (*samāpatti*); this refers to that which is accompanied by craving for concentration, because one develops attachment toward pure concentration."
The second is the ignorance of attachment to the subtle and pure dharmas, which is precisely what is meant here by "concomitant with attachment to the dharmas.
By "pure dharmas" is meant the dharma of *tathatā*, the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), and the twelvefold teaching of the Buddha.
These two types of ignorance constitute the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and are associated with the two kinds of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) among the afflictions.

Furthermore, from time immemorial, these two ignorances have arisen spontaneously within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), arising in association with the two views of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
Now, because ignorance is severed upon entering this stage, both types of craving and both types of view will never again manifest.
The severance of the seeds and the severance of the manifest are to be understood in accordance with what was explained above.

However, that which differs from the preceding stages in this stage is as follows: while the practices of generosity, ethical discipline, and cultivation in the first three stages are identical to those of the mundane world, the fourth stage is now termed "supramundane" because one has attained the untainted factors conducive to enlightenment (*anāsrava-bodhipakṣadharma*).
From this point, the practice of the second stage (*bhūmi*) is explained,
which is divided into three parts.
First, the initial section indicates the practice to be cultivated.
Sūtra: “Cultivate the boundless factors of enlightenment. Commentary:

Regarding "cultivation," as stated in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, it means that within this stage, the aspects of the practices leading to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) cultivated are boundless; alternatively, the benefit to others is boundless, or the progression toward the merit of the fruition is boundless—hence it is called "boundless."

"Bhāga" (part) means cause; it also carries the sense of a constituent member. Because they lead toward the fruit, these factors pertaining to the fruit are called "dharmas of the parts" (bodhipakṣa-dharma).
Following this, the second section clarifies the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa). Sūtra:
"Endowment with the foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of psychic power, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, and the path.
The commentary explains:
Regarding the foundations of mindfulness and so forth, the first three each have four; the next two each have five; the next has seven; and the last has eight, totaling thirty-seven.
The enumeration of names and the identification of their essential natures are as in the preceding "Introduction Chapter.

Since all that is cultivated in this stage is untainted (*anāsrava*), as stated in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* regarding the cultivation of the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and diligence (*vīrya*), each instance specifies the removal of worldly greed and sorrow.

From the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) down to the Eightfold Noble Path, each one is endowed with four aspects: relying on revulsion, relying on detachment, relying on cessation of the mind, and relying on equanimity; as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says, "Dedication toward equanimity."
As the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states: "Wisdom that takes suffering and its origin as its object is called 'disgust' (*nirveda*).
All paths capable of severing the afflictions are called 'detachment' (*virāga*), because they detach one from the afflictions."
"Cessation" (*nirodha*) refers to the absence of afflictions, because the principle of cessation is manifested.
"Relinquishment" (*tyāga*) refers to great equanimity (*mahopekṣā*), because one abides in tranquility.
These are analyzed in detail as found in the twenty-fifth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* and the tenth chapter of the *Abhidharma-samuccaya*.
From this, the third section clarifies the fruit toward which one proceeds.
The Sūtra says:
“In order to accomplish the powers, the fearlessnesses, and the unique qualities of a Buddha.”
The commentary states:
For the purpose of proceeding toward the fruit of Buddhahood, the text is easy to understand.
From here, the second section of the sutra explains the fulfillment of the stages (*bhūmi*).
Sūtra: "For seven asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he cultivated the immeasurable perfection of diligence, remained far removed from indolence, and universally benefited all sentient beings."
The commentary states:
Regarding "seven asaṃkhyeyas," it is as previously added.
As for the term "immeasurable," it refers to the vastness of the various practices; and because one practices and cultivates them without regression, all are characterized by diligence.
This perfection [of vigor] increases preeminently because the others are present only in part;
it distances one from laziness because its obstacles are permanently severed;
and it brings universal benefit to sentient beings because it equally benefits others.
From here begins the eighth stage, the Stage Difficult to Conquer (*Sudurjayā-bhūmi*).
The text is divided into three parts as before; first, the initial section marks the characteristics of entering this stage.
The Sūtra says:

"Furthermore, in the Stage Difficult to Conquer (*Sudurjayā*), the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, by means of the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), accords with the characteristics of true suchness (*tathatā*)—which is pure, equal, and without differentiation—and thereby severs the pursuit of nirvāṇa characteristic of the Lesser Vehicle."
The commentary states:
To clarify the entry into the stages, as the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* says: "For a Bodhisattva of the fifth stage, this sign appears first.
There is a woman of exquisite jewels, her body adorned all over with necklaces of genuine gems, and her head crowned with flowers as ornaments; the Bodhisattva sees them all."

Regarding the "Difficult-to-Conquer Ground" (*Sudurjayā-bhūmi*): because one attains mastery over the superior wisdom of the skillful means of practice—something difficult to attain—it is named the Difficult-to-Conquer Ground.
As for the "four fearlessnesses" (*catur-vaiśāradya*), there are two types:

first, the four fearlessnesses of the fruit of Buddhahood: (1) fearlessness regarding omniscience, (2) fearlessness regarding the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*), (3) fearlessness regarding the obstacles to the path, and (4) fearlessness regarding the path leading out of suffering; these are to be distinguished as explained elsewhere.

Second are the four fearlessnesses of a bodhisattva: first, fearlessness in hearing and retaining; second, fearlessness in liberation; third, fearlessness in the midst of an assembly; and fourth, fearlessness in answering difficult questions, as previously explained.

Regarding the latter four types, they are called "fearlessness" because one aspires to further progress, extensively practices the application of benefit and happiness, and thereby induces entry into this stage.
