"From this point forward, [the text] clarifies the practices cultivated during the stage of Equal Enlightenment.

Regarding the arising of the Vajra Samādhi when about to achieve Perfect Enlightenment, both the twelfth fascicle of the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* and the thirty-ninth fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* state: "When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva enters the Stage of Receiving the Empowerment (*abhiṣeka-bhūmi*), one million asaṃkhyeya samādhis already attained manifest before him; the final of these samādhis is named 'Receiving the Supreme Position of All-Knowledge' (*sarvajñatā-abhiṣeka-adhikāra*)."

When this samādhi manifests, a great precious lotus flower suddenly appears; the flower is vast, its magnitude equaling a million triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems. It is adorned with various exquisite jewels interspersed throughout, surpassing all mundane realms, and arises from supramundane roots of goodness. It constantly emits light that universally illumines the Dharma-realm, with lotus flowers as numerous as the atoms within a triple-thousand great thousandfold world system serving as its retinue.
At that time, the Bodhisattva’s body was exceptionally sublime as he sat upon this flower-throne, his physical proportions being perfectly harmonious.

Immeasurable bodhisattvas served as his retinue, each seated upon other lotus flowers, surrounding him on all sides; every one of them had individually attained a million samādhis and gazed with single-minded devotion toward the Great Bodhisattva.
The radiance and the speech of this Great Bodhisattva, together with his retinue, pervaded and filled the Dharma-realm in the ten directions.
All worlds shook, the evil realms were stilled, and the lands became adorned and pure; all bodhisattvas of like practice gathered there without exception.

From the soles of his feet, this Great Bodhisattva emits light that illuminates all the hells; from his kneecaps, he emits light that illuminates all the animal realms; from his navel, he emits light that illuminates the realm of Yama; from his two flanks, he emits light that illuminates all human destinies; from his two hands, he emits light that illuminates the devas and asuras; from his two shoulders, he emits light that universally illuminates the śrāvakas; from the back of his neck, he emits light that illuminates the pratyekabuddhas; from his face, he emits light that illuminates bodhisattvas from their first aspiration up to the ninth stage; from between his eyebrows, he emits light that universally illuminates the bodhisattvas receiving empowerment throughout the ten directions; and from the crown of his head, he emits light that universally illuminates the sites of enlightenment of all Buddhas in all worlds throughout the ten directions.
Circumambulating ten times, they stayed in mid-air, forming a lattice of light and raining down ornaments as an offering.
Circumambulating another ten times, they entered through the soles of the feet of all the Tathāgatas.

At that time, all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, knowing that a certain Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva in a certain world had arrived to receive his position of succession, all came to observe him, and each of those Bodhisattvas immediately attained ten thousand samādhis.

From between the eyebrows of all Buddhas, light emanates, universally illuminating all worlds in the ten directions; it circles to the right ten times, manifesting buddha-activities, and arrives at this assembly of bodhisattvas. Having circled to the right and manifested various kinds of adornments, the light enters through the crowns of the great bodhisattvas. They thereby attain millions of samādhis previously unattained, which is called "having attained the rank of consecration."
It is like the crown prince born to a Universal Monarch (cakravartin), whose mother is the principal queen and who is endowed with all the physical marks of excellence.

The king places the prince upon a magnificent golden throne atop a precious white elephant, while canopies, banners, and streamers are displayed, flowers are scattered, and music is performed. He takes water from the four great oceans and places it within a golden vase; the king then holds this vase and pours the water over the prince’s head, at which moment he is said to have received the royal position.
It is as explained extensively in that [text].

Now, regarding the phrase "when the vajra-samādhi manifests before one," it refers to what was stated in the preceding sutra: "one attains the final samādhi among the one million samādhis previously unattained."
Based on this supreme concentration (*samādhi*), one gives rise to the path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*) to sever subtle hindrances.
This has two meanings. Some say:
This refers to the abandonment of the obstacles to the eleventh stage, the Tathāgata-bhūmi, which consists of two types of ignorance. As stated in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*:
first, there is the ignorance that constitutes a subtle obstruction to all objects of knowledge, which is precisely the subtle cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) mentioned here;

second, there is the ignorance consisting of the coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*) of extremely subtle afflictions, which is precisely the seed of all spontaneously arising afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) mentioned here.

These two types of ignorance obstruct the stage of Buddhahood; because they are abandoned at the time of the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), both the seeds and the manifest states of the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) are relinquished.
Those who maintain that [the abandonment] occurs at different times claim it is because the seeds are abandoned;
those who maintain it is simultaneous claim it is because [the manifest state] has not yet been abandoned.

Some say: Regarding "severance," as stated in the *Awakening of Faith*, it is only the mental characteristics (*citta-lakṣaṇa*) that cease, not the essence of mind (*citta-tattva*). "Cessation" here means severance.
The essence of mind, in its own characteristic, functions as a whole to give rise to ignorance; this is to stir the quiescent and cause it to move, not to transform non-existence into existence.

The cause of the mind’s movement is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*), which arises as the characteristic of activity (*karmalakṣaṇa*). Now, at the stage of Perfect Enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*), the fundamental ignorance is severed; when ignorance is exhausted, the characteristic of movement is extinguished accordingly. Thus, while the mental characteristics are extinguished, the essence of the mind (*cittatattva*) is not extinguished.

Regarding the distinction between these two: the former involves the severance of the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), while the latter involves the severance of the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*); thus, taking both texts together, their meanings are consistent.
As for the phrase "yet not yet equal to those who are equal to the unequaled," this stage is inferior and therefore has not yet attained equality with the Buddha.
The Buddha transcends these stages; therefore, he is called "Incomparable" (asama).
Since the path of every Buddha is equal, he is called "Equal to the Equal" (samasama).
From this second point, a simile is raised to explain and establish this.
Sūtra: "For example, it is as if there were a person who ascended a very high terrace and surveyed everything, understanding all things without exception. Explanation:
"Ascending the high terrace" refers to dwelling prominently upon its summit;
because the Bodhisattva’s rank is ultimate, it is like that summit.
From this point, the second section clarifies the stage of Buddhahood.

Sūtra: "In the state of liberation, there is a single mark which is markless; it is without arising and without cessation, identical to the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and equal to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā). Having fulfilled the treasury of merit, one abides in the stage of the Tathāgata."
The commentary states:
Regarding the phrase "if [they are] equal to liberation," there are two meanings.
The former master explains it as follows:
This is also the path of liberation.

This is because the seeds and manifestations of the fundamental consciousness, as well as the inferior outflows, are abandoned and relinquished by the uninterrupted path and the path of liberation that sever subtle obstacles, exactly as previously explained.
As stated in the third fascicle of the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*: "Regarding the attainment of the mental states of the four wisdoms at which stage:

although the seeds of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) are originally present, they first manifest at this stage of liberation (*vimukti*). All the untainted (*anāsrava*) seeds of the Buddha-fruit are fully perfected and dependent [upon it], remaining constant and uninterrupted throughout the limits of the future."

The category of the Wisdom of Equality (samatājñāna) manifests in the first bhūmi; it is cultivated and increased in each subsequent bhūmi. As the fruit of the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (dharmanairātmyajñāna), it is constantly manifest, though it is interrupted during moments of impure (sāsrava) mind. This continues until the final moment of mind at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samabhisambodhi), where it remains perpetually uninterrupted throughout the limits of the future. This is because, just as the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) is always co-present during the impure state, this [wisdom] is established as being ever-present and uninterrupted within that [state].

The wisdom of wondrous observation also first manifests at this stage; from this point onward, it is gradually cultivated and increased until the fruit of Buddhahood, where it no longer functions even when entering the meditative absorption of cessation.
Regarding the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), some say that it manifests in its entirety from the first bhūmi onward.

According to the true meaning, however, it arises only at the stage of Buddhahood; for it has never been observed that the five contaminated faculties (*sāsrava-indriya*) give rise to uncontaminated consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*), and because such wisdom may be subject to interruption during the stages leading up to Buddhahood.
To speak of "one characteristic" means that the pure dharma-realm has the single characteristic of suchness.
To speak of "no characteristic" means that the mental states of the four wisdoms realize suchness according to their respective capacities, which is eternally without characteristics.
Regarding "neither arising nor ceasing": although the essence of the wisdom that realizes suchness (*tathatā*) continues in succession, it is always conjoined with suchness without interruption.
Regarding "identical with the limit of reality" (*bhūtakoṭi*): this is because the wisdom is equal to suchness.
"Equal in the nature of phenomena (dharmatā)" means that it is unchanging.
"Fulfilling the treasury of merit" means that the conditioned merits fulfill the body of wisdom-virtue, while the unconditioned merits are inherently fulfilled by their very nature.
Abiding in the stage of the Tathāgata is the ground of fulfillment.

Regarding the differentiation of the bodies: that which is realized is the Truth Body (*svabhāvakāya*), while the four wisdoms that realize it are the Self-Enjoyment Body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*). Although within the resultant state there is no distinction between subject and object, the five dharmas are categorized as belonging to these two bodies.

The outflowing merit consists of the two bodies that benefit others; these differ in terms of coarseness and subtlety according to whether they pertain to the stages prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*) or the stages upon the grounds.

The power of the great compassionate vow is equal and non-dual, yet what is perceived by various classes of beings differs in superiority or inferiority. These two bodies are neither identical to nor separate from one's own [Dharmakāya].
As explained at length in that [text], the subsequent master’s liberation is the same as before.

Regarding the term "single characteristic" (*ekalakṣaṇa*): whereas the preceding path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantaryamārga*) extinguished the fundamental ignorance, the present path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) returns the mind to its original source; thus, they share a single characteristic.
It is called "signless" because all signs are absent.
It is "without arising and without ceasing" because wisdom is in profound stillness with ultimate truth, being free from arising and ceasing.
It "shares the same limit as reality" because the characteristics of movement have been extinguished.
"Equal to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā)" means that wisdom is equal to suchness.
"Fulfilling the treasury of merit" means that the essence of spiritual understanding is perfected.
"Abiding in the stage of the Tathāgata" means being quiescent and immovable.
Regarding the distinctions of the body: first is the greatness of essence (*tattva-mahat*), because the true essence is all-pervasive;
second is the greatness of attributes (*lakṣaṇa-mahat*), because the inherent virtues are perfect;
third is the greatness of function (*vṛtti-mahat*), because it pervades the dharma-realm, being active yet eternally quiescent, neither identical with nor separate from [the essence].
The former dispatch establishes identity, while the latter dispatch establishes difference; as these aspects mutually illuminate one another, they are not contradictory.
This concludes the thirteenth section, the Dharma Master’s summary and fulfillment of the positions.
Although the fruit of Buddhahood is clarified, it is not treated separately because it is presented within the final stage among the three stages of the Sages (trayaḥ-ārya-pudgalāḥ).
Second, the conclusion and the formal commitment to uphold [the teaching] are stated.
This section is divided into two parts:
First, the formal declaration of faith and understanding.
First, regarding the initial formal declaration of upholding [the teaching],
the sutra states:

“Good son! Such bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as these, who uphold, explain, and practice [this teaching], go to all the buddha-fields of the ten directions to benefit and bring peace to sentient beings and to penetrate the true nature of reality, no different from myself today.”
The commentary states:
"Phrases such as these" serve as a summary of the preceding section.

Regarding the practice of receiving, upholding, explaining, and propagating [this teaching] throughout the buddha-fields, although there are vast differences in the degree of benefit and joy bestowed compared to that of the Buddhas themselves, because the aspects of transformation and benefit are shared equally, it is said that they are no different.
From this point, the second section establishes faith and understanding.
It is divided into two parts:
first, the prose exposition reveals it; second, the verses further clarify it.
Furthermore, first, the prose section of the sutra reveals this:
"O son of good family!..."
All Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the entire Dharma-realm have attained Buddhahood by relying upon this gate.
If one claims that Buddhahood can be attained by transcending this, it is the teaching of Māra, not the teaching of the Buddha.
"Therefore, you all should know thus, see thus, and believe and understand thus.
The commentary states:
"All rely upon this gate" indicates that they practice together.
If one says that anything exceeding these [categories] was not spoken by the Buddha, then the term "equal" (sama) is intended to encourage the arising of correct understanding.

Regarding "knowledge and vision" (*jñānadarśana*), as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "If wisdom (*jñāna*) relies upon *śamatha*, it is 'knowledge'; if it relies upon *vipaśyanā*, it is 'vision'."
These two rely upon samādhi; therefore, they are called "resolute belief" (adhimokṣa).
Because the activity of samādhi is sovereign, one understands internal objects of focus; since there are mental images, that is termed "supreme resolve" (adhimukti).
From this point, the second section explains the verses in further detail.
